prompt: What does this course need from you before its first exercise?

choices.text: A Google Play developer account
choices.why: Lesson 3 explains the account; no exercise depends on having one.

choices.text: A Mac with Xcode for the iOS lessons
choices.why: The iOS half is read, and nothing in the course depends on a Mac.

choices.text: A computer with the tools of this lesson
choices.why: Right. Node, a JDK and the Android command-line tools; no account, card or phone.

choices.text: An Android phone in developer mode
choices.why: Nothing is installed on a phone in this course.

prompt: Lesson 2 is about signing an iPhone app. Why is most of it read rather than practised?

choices.text: Apple's build tools run only on macOS
choices.why: Right. Xcode and the codesigning it does need a Mac, which the recording machine was not.

choices.text: Apple forbids signing outside its consoles
choices.why: Signing happens on your Mac, with Xcode; the console is not where it runs.

choices.text: iOS certificates are too expensive for a course
choices.why: The membership costs money, but the reason for reading is the operating system, not the fee.

choices.text: Swift does not compile on Linux
choices.why: Swift does compile on Linux; Xcode and its signing do not exist there.

prompt: `apksigner --version` printed 0.9, and the build tools you installed are 36.0.0. What went wrong?

choices.text: An old apksigner is earlier on the PATH
choices.why: That would be a problem, but 0.9 is what the current build tools print.

choices.text: sdkmanager installed the wrong package
choices.why: `--list_installed` showed build-tools 36.0.0.

choices.text: The JDK is too new for the build tools
choices.why: JDK 21 runs them; the version shown is apksigner's own.

choices.text: Nothing: apksigner numbers itself separately
choices.why: Right. The tool has its own version, and both numbers are correct.

prompt: Put the setup of the Android tools in order.
items: Unpack it and rename the folder to `latest`
Add the two lines to `~/.profile` and open a new terminal

prompt: What does the signature on an Android app prove?

choices.text: That Google checked the app for malware
choices.why: No authority stands behind the certificate; you made it yourself.

choices.text: That every version was signed by the same key holder
choices.why: Right. That is the fact an update is checked against.

choices.text: That the developer's identity was verified
choices.why: The name in `-dname` is never checked by anybody.

choices.text: That the code has not changed since the first release
choices.why: Every update changes the code; the key is what stays.

prompt: Match each change to what a phone with the old version does.

pairs.left: a new icon and new code
pairs.right: installs the update, keeping the data

right_distractors: asks the person which key to trust

prompt: Sign-in with Google works in the debug build of the planner and fails in the release build installed from the Play Store. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The release build was minified and lost the sign-in code
choices.why: Minification renames code; it does not change which certificate Google sees.

choices.text: Only the debug key's fingerprint was registered
choices.why: Right. The store build is signed by Google's app signing key, whose fingerprint has to be registered too.

choices.text: The package name differs between debug and release
choices.why: It would fail too, but a release from the store keeps the published package name.

choices.text: Google services refuse apps installed from a store
choices.why: They accept them; they check the fingerprint they were given.

prompt: Put the steps of a signed APK in the order the lesson ran them.
Why does `zipalign` run before `apksigner sign` and not after it?

choices.text: The order does not matter
choices.why: It does: aligning after signing invalidates the signature.

choices.text: apksigner refuses a package bigger than 4 KB
choices.why: There is no such limit; the signed package was over 12 KB.

choices.text: zipalign needs the password
choices.why: zipalign never touches the key.

choices.text: Aligning moves bytes, which would break a signature over them
choices.why: Right. v2 and v3 sign the whole file, so it has to be final first.

prompt: To keep the password out of the shell's history, the lesson reads it into a variable and passes it to apksigner as `--ks-pass ___:UPLOAD_PASS`.
Your laptop, with the planner's upload keystore on it, is stolen. The app uses Play App Signing. What happens to the people who have the app?

choices.text: Nothing: you ask for an upload key reset and carry on
choices.why: Right. Phones never saw the upload key.

choices.text: Their next update fails until they reinstall
choices.why: Their phones check Google's key, which did not change.

choices.text: The app is removed from sale until a new listing is made
choices.why: That was the end of an app whose only key was lost, before Play held keys.

choices.text: Google sends you a copy of the upload key
choices.why: Google never had your upload key; it holds only its certificate.

prompt: Which of these does the holder of the upload key do? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Signs the .aab before uploading it
choices.why: Right. That is the upload key's one job.

choices.text: Signs the APKs phones install
choices.why: Google does that, with the app signing key.

choices.text: Keeps the keystore and its password backed up apart
choices.why: Right. Two places that cannot fail together.

choices.text: Gives the private key to services such as Firebase
choices.why: Services get a fingerprint, never a private key.

prompt: In the lesson, `apksigner` named `CN=Play stand-in` on the APK built by bundletool. Why not the upload certificate that signed the bundle?

choices.text: bundletool removed the upload signature because it was self-signed
choices.why: Being self-signed is normal for both keys; that is not why.

choices.text: The bundle was never signed
choices.why: `jarsigner -verify` said `jar verified`.

choices.text: Whoever builds the APKs signs them
choices.why: Right. The APKs are new files, signed by the key given to the tool that made them.

choices.text: apksigner shows the newest key in the keystore
choices.why: apksigner reads the APK, not a keystore.

prompt: `keytool -list` answers `keystore password was incorrect`. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The password is wrong or the file is damaged
choices.why: Right. The message is the same for both.

choices.text: That the password is wrong, and the file is intact
choices.why: keytool says the same for a damaged file; it cannot tell the two apart.

choices.text: That the JDK is missing
choices.why: Then keytool would not have run at all.

choices.text: That the key has expired
choices.why: Expiry is not checked when listing a keystore.

prompt: Google Play refuses a key whose validity ends before 22 October 2033. A key made on 30 October 2026 with `-validity 2500` lasts how many whole years, rounded down?
A colleague suggests committing the upload keystore to the private repository, so the pipeline can find it. What is the problem?

choices.text: Git cannot store binary files
choices.why: It can; that is not the issue.

choices.text: The pipeline cannot read files from the repository
choices.why: It can; that is exactly why the idea is tempting.

choices.text: It stays in every clone made since, and removing it later does not reach them
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 keeps it as an encrypted secret of the pipeline instead.

choices.text: The keystore would be signed again on every commit
choices.why: A keystore is not signed by commits.

prompt: A React Native student asks whether Play App Signing applies to them. What is the answer?

choices.text: No: Expo signs JavaScript apps with its own key
choices.why: EAS can hold your upload key, but Google still holds the app signing key.

choices.text: Yes: the Android build is a normal Android project with the same two keys
choices.why: Right. The JavaScript ships inside a native app, signed like any other.

choices.text: Only for apps written in Kotlin
choices.why: Play signs what it distributes, whatever language built it.

choices.text: No: JavaScript bundles are not signed
choices.why: The JavaScript is inside the APK, and the APK is signed.

prompt: Which of these makes a phone refuse the planner's next update?

choices.text: A new upload key, after a reset
choices.why: Phones never see the upload key.

choices.text: Dropping the v1 scheme from the signature
choices.why: A phone on Android 7.0 or later checks v2 and v3.

choices.text: A new versionName with the same versionCode as before
choices.why: That is refused by Google Play on upload, before any phone sees it.

choices.text: An APK signed by a different app signing key
choices.why: Right. The certificate on the update has to match the installed one.
